stem: Which of the following is NOT typically associated with school refusal?
explanation: School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, even when under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatric disorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than a diagnosis. School refusal is generally  associated with separation anxiety and may co-occur with anxiety and depressive disorders. It is usually not an isolated problem. These children typically avoid many other social situations, and often display tantrums, desperate pleas, and somatic complaints (e.g. headaches, stomach aches, nausea). School refusal may occur in a young child who is first entering school or in an older child or adolescent who is making a transition into a new grade or school.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 896. Elliott JG, Place M. Practitioner review: school refusal: developments in conceptualisation and treatment since 2000. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. 2019 Jan;60(1):4-15.

stem: Which of the following is true about Tourette syndrome?
options: Mean age of onset is 12 years
Females are more affected than males
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 6 months
Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months
Antipsychotics are the first line treatment
correctAnswer: Diagnosed by having both motor and vocal tics for 12 months 
explanation: Tourette syndrome is a complex neuropsychiatric disorder with childhood onset characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, present for at least a year. Males are more commonly affected (3-4:1, male:female). The age of onset is 2-21 years, with a mean age of 7  years. All patients should receive psychoeducation, reassurance, and explanation. In mild cases and young people this may suffice. Behavioural methods (that may be useful alone or in combination with medications) include habit reversal training, comprehensive behavioural intervention for tics, exposure and response prevention, and self-hypnosis. Medication is warranted if tics cause distress or are functionally disabling and is also used in the treatment of many of the co-morbidities.
reference: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75. Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. p. 587.

stem: Which one of the following is a true statement about bipolar disorder in children and adolescents?
options: 60-70% of initial presentations are a manic episode
Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features
Lamotrigine is used if treatment resistant manic episodes are present
The course is often episodic and of brief duration
correctAnswer:
Manic children typically present with atypical or mixed features




explanation: Children experiencing a manic episode typically present with atypical or mixed features characterised by irritability, labile mood, and behavioural problems. Periods of depression are common, and early-onset bipolar disorder more often presents with depression than in  adult-onset bipolar. Early-onset bipolar may be characterised by non-episodic, chronic, ultra-rapid cycling, mixed irritable and manic states. The prevalence in adolescents is approximately 1% and as high as 6% when including soft subsyndromal symptoms. M>F in childhood cases; M=F in adolescents. For the treatment of mania and hypomania in youth, NICE guidelines suggest following the same recommendations as adults: second-generation antipsychotics (SGAs) may be used as first-line treatment, and mood stabilisers can be added after failure of two trials of SGAs. Lamotrigine has not been studied in RCTs for the treatment of acute bipolar depression in children and adolescents and is not recommended as first-line. It is not recommended in the treatment of manic episodes.
reference: Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective. stem: In operant conditioning with children, shaping refers to
options: Reinforcing positive behaviour; ignoring negative behaviour
Punishing negative behaviour; praising positive behaviour
Neither reinforcing nor punishing observed behaviours
Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome
Differential reinforcement of behaviours other than the desired outcome
correctAnswer:
Gradual reinforcement of behaviours approximating the desired outcome


explanation: Shaping is used to produce a complex behaviour that is not in the child’s initial repertoire. Initially, component parts of the desired behaviour are rewarded, then reward is limited to behaviour that approximates the desired outcome. As appropriate behaviour appears, it  is rewarded only if it is ‘in the right direction’, and further reward is contingent upon continued advancement until the child is only rewarded once the entire behaviour is performed.

explanation: Reactive attachment disorder (RAD) is characterised by grossly abnormal attachment behaviours in early childhood, occurring in the context of a history of grossly inadequate child care (e.g. severe neglect, maltreatment, institutional deprivation). Even when an adequate primary  caregiver is newly available, the child does not turn to the primary caregiver for comfort, support, and nurture; rarely displays security- seeking behaviours towards any adult; and does not respond when comfort is offered. RAD can only be diagnosed in children, and features of the disorder develop within the first 5 years of life. However, the disorder cannot be diagnosed before the age of 1 (or a developmental age of less than 9 months), when the capacity for selective attachments may not be fully developed, or in the context of autism spectrum disorder.
reference: International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (11th ed. ICD-11; World Health Organization, 2020)

stem: Which one of the following is a good prognostic factor in children with conduct disorder?
options: Having a family member convicted for violent conduct
explanation: Protective factors conferring a better prognosis include 1. Female gender 2. High IQ 3. Resilient temperament 4. Good parenting among several others. Werner's (1992, 1994) longitudinal study investigated resilience in over 200 babies born in 1955 on a Hawaiian island, following and assessing the children at various times up to the age of 32 years. Werner found that the resilient children - those with the ability to cope with the internal stresses of their vulnerabilities and the external stresses of their environment - had low rates of variously  defined conduct problems.

stem: Regarding the aetiology of ADHD, all of the following are true except
options: There is a 50% increased risk in monozygotic twins
Siblings of hyperactive children have about twice the increased risk of having the disorder
Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex
Neuroimaging shows lower cerebral blood flow and metabolic rates in the frontal lobe areas of children with ADHD than in controls
correctAnswer:
Predominant serotonin dysregulation is seen in the prefrontal cortex


explanation: Many neurotransmitters are likely associated with ADHD symptoms. However, dopamine is a primary focus of clinical investigation, and the prefrontal cortex has been implicated based on its role in attention and regulation of impulse control. Studies have also shown that brain  regions such as the locus coeruleus, which consists predominantly of noradrenergic neurons, play a significant role in attention. In part, hypotheses regarding the neurochemistry of ADHD have arisen from the effect of medications. Stimulants, known to be the most effective medications in the treatment of ADHD, affect both dopamine and norepinephrine, leading to neurotransmitter hypotheses that may include dysfunction in both the adrenergic and dopaminergic systems.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 139.

stem: Pica typically occurs during
explanation: Pica is characterised by the persistent (>1month) eating of non-nutritive substances at a developmentally inappropriate age (>1 year). It typically occurs during the 2nd and 3rd years of life, though may occur in young pregnant women. Common substances include dirt, stones,  plastic, paper, hair, faeces, wood, string, etc. Pica is common in people with intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder. Consequences may include toxicity, infection, or GIT ulceration/obstruction. Hypothesized causes include hunger, malnutrition, nutritional deficiencies, psychosocial stressors, and brain disorders such as lesions in the hypothalamus.
reference: Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 694.

stem: A 14-year-old girl presents with some uncoordinated movements of her limbs and emotional lability. She has a history of fever and sore throat six months ago. Which is the most likely cause for her presentation?
explanation: Sydenham chorea is the major neurological presentation of rheumatic fever, an inflammatory process following infection with group A  streptococci (GAS) such as throat infection or scarlet fever. Sydenham chorea is characterised by uncoordinated jerking movements affecting the face and limbs, as well as hypotonia. Some children also experience vocal and motor tics that may persist. Behavioural symptoms and psychiatric co-morbidities are common and can have an abrupt onset that may precede the onset of the chorea. Emotional lability, anxiety, and symptoms of OCD are the most well recognised and there have also been associations with ADHD, mood disorders, and even symptoms of psychosis.
reference: Warrilow A, Morton M. Autoimmune disorders in child psychiatry: keeping up with the field. BJPsych Advances. 2015 Nov;21(6):367-76.

stem: Manifestations of oppositional defiant disorder are almost invariably present
options: In the presence of all adults
explanation: In oppositional defiant disorder (ODD), a child’s temper outbursts, active refusal to comply with rules, and annoying behaviours exceed expectations for these behaviours for children of the same age. The disorder is an enduring pattern of negativistic, hostile, and defiant  behaviours in the absence of significant violations of the rights of others. Manifestations of ODD are almost invariably present in the home, but they may not be present at school or with other adults or peers. In some cases, the child has symptoms outside the home from the start. In others, it starts at home and later moves beyond that. Typically, symptoms of the disorder are most evident in interactions with adults or peers whom the child knows well.
reference: Boland R, Verduin M. Kaplan and Sadock's Synopsis of Psychiatry, 12th Edition. 2022. p. 187.

stem: Which of the following has been found to be effective in treating adolescent inhalant abuse?
explanation: Adolescent inhalant abuse is characterised by the use of gases, glues, and/or aerosols to achieve intoxication. Inhalants are frequently one of the first drugs to be used by adolescents due to ease of access, lack of penalties association with possession, and rapid onset of effects.  First-line treatment for adolescent inhalant abuse is multimodal, including individual CBT, family therapy, and activity and engagement programs.

stem: Which of the following should be used as a first choice treatment in adolescents with acute manic or mixed episodes?
explanation: Aripiprazole and lithium are the only licensed medications for treating mania. In practice, lithium is not generally used acutely in the treatment of manic/mixed episodes in adolescents, as it requires commitment to longer-term treatment and regular blood tests. NICE  guidelines (updated 2020) recommend considering aripiprazole or using an alternative antipsychotic (e.g. risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine) in accordance with guidance for adults and limiting drug treatment to 12 weeks. It is unclear whether valproate has the same beneficial effects on mania in young people as it does in adults. NICE recommends that valproate monotherapy should NOT be used for first-line management of mania and it should NOT be offered to girls or young women of childbearing potential because of teratogenic effects and the risk of polycystic ovary syndrome.
reference: National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. The NICE guideline on the assessment and management of bipolar disorder in adults, children and young people in primary and secondary care. Updated edition 2020. Findling RL et al. Progress in diagnosis and treatment of bipolar disorder among children and adolescents: an international perspective.  Evidence-based mental health. 2018 Nov 1;21(4):177-81.

stem: Which neurotransmitter system is commonly postulated to be involved in the aetiology of Tourette syndrome?
explanation: The aetiology of Tourette syndrome includes genetic factors and environmental influences (infections and neuroimmunological effects, pre- and/or perinatal difficulties, psychosocial stressors, and androgen influences). No single gene has been identified (likely more than one  gene). An association with psychosocial stress is well known. Heightened HPA axis and noradrenergic system reactivity have been demonstrated. There is a likely disturbance of the dopamine system. Other aetiological possibilities include gestational and perinatal insults, exposure to androgens, heat, fatigue, and post-infectious autoimmune mechanisms.
reference: Robertson MM. Tourette syndrome in children and adolescents: aetiology, presentation and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 May;22(3):165-75. Semple D, Smyth R. Oxford handbook of psychiatry. Oxford university press; 2019 Jul 30. p. 676.

explanation: School refusal is characterised by refusal to go to school or stay in school, even when under pressure from parents and school authorities. It is not a psychiatric disorder per se and can have many causes; it is considered a problem rather than a diagnosis. School refusal may occur  in a young child who is first entering school or in an older child or adolescent who is making a transition into a new grade or school. The peak age is 11-13 years. The incidence in children and adolescents reported to be 1-5%, with the sex distribution equal.

Developmental learning disorder with impairment in written expression
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics
Developmental learning disorder with impairment in reading
Developmental language disorder with impairment of mainly expressive language
correctAnswer: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics 
explanation: Developmental learning disorder with impairment in mathematics is characterised by significant and persistent difficulties in learning academic skills related to mathematics or arithmetic, such as number sense, memorisation of number facts, accurate calculation, fluent  calculation, and accurate mathematic reasoning. The individual’s performance in mathematics or arithmetic is markedly below what would be expected for chronological or developmental age and level of intellectual functioning and results in significant impairment in functioning. 1-6% of school-age children are affected, with female predominance. It is often associated with visuospatial deficits and attributed to right parietal dysfunction.

explanation: Rates of suicide in the UK have increased among adolescents by approximately 7.9% each year between 2010 and 2017. stem: Developmentally inappropriate social relatedness seen before the age of 5 following prolonged separation from caregivers is seen in
explanation: Disinhibited social engagement disorder is newly described in both DSM-5 and ICD-11. It is characterised by a pattern of behaviour in which a child actively approaches and interacts with unfamiliar adults in an overly familiar way. These children may display reduced/absent  reticence in approaching/interacting with unfamiliar adults; overly familiar verbal of physical behaviour; diminished/absent checking back with an adult caregiver; and willingness to go off with unfamiliar adults with little to no hesitation. These children have experienced patterns of extremes of insufficient care (e.g. social neglect or deprivation, repeated changes of primary caregivers, rearing in institutions or other settings that severely limit opportunities to form selective attachment).

stem: What genetic aetiology most increases the risk of parents having a second child with Down syndrome?
explanation: In translocation, a fusion occurs of two chromosomes, usually 21 and 15, resulting in a total of 46 chromosomes, despite the presence of one extra chromosome 21. Unlike trisomy 21, this is usually inherited, and the translocated chromosome may be found in unaffected  parents or siblings (who only have 45 chromosomes).

stem: Which one of the following is not recommended in the management of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents?
explanation: For the treatment of anxiety disorders in children and adolescents, psychoeducation can help families understand the condition and provide reassurance. CBT has been proven to be effective, incorporating both cognitive (e.g. reframing, positive self-talk, challenging unhelpful  thoughts, and weighing up evidence for and against expected events) and behavioural processes (e.g. systematic desensitisation, exposure and response prevention for specific phobias, relaxation training, modelling, rewarding wanted behaviour, and role-play). Family therapy may help when dysfunctional patterns of family interaction influence the child’s anxiety symptoms. SSRIs can be effective and are generally well-tolerated. Medication is usually most considered in older children with more severe symptoms. Benzodiazepines have NOT shown efficacy; their side effects (e.g. behavioural disinhibition) are a risk in this population.
reference: Vallance AK, Fernandez V. Anxiety disorders in children and adolescents: aetiology, diagnosis and treatment. BJPsych Advances. 2016 Sep;22(5):335-44.

correctAnswer: Enuresis may occur in association with a mental disorder or psychosocial stressor
explanation: In ICD-11, enuresis is defined as the repeated voiding of urine into clothes or bed, which may occur during the day or at night, in an individual who has reached a developmental age when urinary continence is ordinarily expected (5 years). The urinary incontinence may  have been present from birth (i.e., an atypical extension of normal infantile incontinence), or may have arisen following a period of acquired bladder control (‘secondary’ or ‘previously dry’ enuresis). The common age of onset for children who have previously acquired urinary continence, yet develop enuresis, is between the ages of 5 to 8 years. Nocturnal enuresis is more common in males, whereas diurnal enuresis is more common in females. Enuresis may be an aspect of another mental, behavioural, or neurodevelopmental disorder. Psychosocial stressors appear to precipitate enuresis in a subgroup of children with the disorder. In young children, the disorder may relate to the birth of a sibling, hospitalisation, the start of school, separation of a family due to divorce, or a move to a new environment.

stem: Which of the following is NOT a core diagnostic feature of ADHD?

stem: In the UK, which of the following drugs should be prescribed first in the treatment of obsessive-compulsive disorder in childhood?
explanation: Sertraline (from age 6 years) and fluvoxamine (from age 8 years) are the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) licensed in the UK for the treatment of OCD in young people. Studies spanning 20 years have established the efficacy of SSRIs in the paediatric population in  placebo-controlled trials. Sertraline and fluoxetine are equally effective, but fluvoxamine may be less so. Paroxetine is not recommended for use in children and young people. On occasion, medications other than sertraline and fluvoxamine may be used as ‘off-label’ preparations with suitable caution. NICE guidance for the treatment of OCD recommends the use of SSRIs before the use of clomipramine, because of clomipramine’s propensity for side effects and need for cardiac monitoring.
reference: Taylor DM, Barnes TRE, Young AH. The Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines in Psychiatry, 14th Edition. 2021. pp. 561-562. National Institute for Health and Clinical Excellence. explanation: The chief differential medical problem to be excluded in children with encopresis is aganglionic megacolon or Hirschsprung disease, in which a patient may have an empty rectum and no desire to defecate but may still have an overflow of feces. explanation: Enuresis is the repeated voiding of urine into a child's clothes or bed; the voiding may be involuntary or intentional. For the diagnosis to be made, a child must exhibit a developmental or chronological age of at least 5 years. Genetic factors play a role in the expression of enuresis,  given that the emergence of enuresis is significantly higher in first-degree relatives. A child’s risk for enuresis is more than seven times higher if their father was enuretic. A classical conditioning behavioural intervention with the bell (or buzzer) and pad (alarm) apparatus is generally the most effective treatment for nocturnal enuresis. explanation:
1) PANDAS syndrome: Paediatric autoimmune neurological disorder associated with streptococcus. An autoimmune syndrome associated with OCD and tic disorder. Some children appear to develop obsessive-compulsive symptoms associated with beta haemolytic streptococcal infection and this presentation represents a small proportion of OCD cases in this population. This association has led to the studies of  immune responses in OCD. Specific characteristics include onset before puberty, episodic or 'sawtooth' course and choreiform movements.

2) Tourette's syndrome is characterised by multiple motor and one or more vocal tics, causing distress and impaired function. The tics occur many times a day (usually in bouts) nearly every day or intermittently throughout a period of more than one year. During this period, there was never a tic-free period of more than three consecutive months. Facial tics: eye blinks or head jerks are often the initial symptoms, but tics involving the neck, shoulders, and upper extremities are also common. 3) Transient tic disorder: Single or multiple motor and/ or vocal tics (sudden, rapid, recurrent, nonrhythmic, stereotyped motor movements or vocalisations). Usually, face, nose, throat are involved (grimaces, blinks, frowns, grunts, throat clearing, sniffs). It is characterized by symptoms from  each of the following three categories: Qualitative impairment in social interaction, Impairment in communication [language delay is most common cause for initial referral], Restricted repetitive and stereotyped patterns of behaviour or interests. 70% have mild to moderate learning disability.

2) Asperger's syndrome is characterised by severe persistent impairment in social interactions, repetitive behaviour patterns, and restricted interests. IQ and language are normal. Unlike autistic disorder, in Asperger's syndrome no significant delays occur in language, cognitive development, or age-appropriate self-help skills. 3) Rett's syndrome is an X linked dominant disorder of arrested Neuro-development, which affects almost exclusively females. Head circumference is normal at birth. Developmental milestones are unremarkable in early life. Between the ages of 6 months to 2 years, head growth begins to decelerate and produces microcephaly. Other signs often include the loss of purposeful hand movements, which are replaced by stereotypic motions, such as hand wringing; the loss of previously acquired speech; psychomotor retardation; and ataxia. Other stereotypical hand movements may occur, such as licking or biting the fingers and tapping or slapping. 4) Childhood disintegrative disorder (CDD) is also called Heller's syndrome and disintegrative psychosis. It is characterised by a marked regression in several areas of functioning after at least two years of apparently normal development. There is normal development for 2-3 years, followed by a loss of acquired motor, language, and social skills between ages three and four years. Stereotypies and compulsions are common.
